job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

response.passage: In a bustling classroom in Pune, Mr. Sharma stood before his students, Rohan and Meera. 'Today, we explore why a compass needle deflects near a wire,' he explained. Rohan pointed to a diagram on the wall showing Hans Oersted, who first noticed this in 1820. 'Is it because the wire gets hot?' Rohan asked. Mr. Sharma shook his head. 'No, the deflection happens because the electric current creates a magnetic field around the wire.' Meera looked at her notes. 'So, does the magnetic field create the current?' she asked. Mr. Sharma smiled. 'Not quite, Meera. The flow of electrons is the cause, and the magnetic effect is the result.' He then mentioned that 15 students from the 2023 batch had built a simple electromagnet using a copper coil. 'Remember,' he added, 'while iron is strongly attracted, not all metals behave like magnets.' Rohan looked at the copper wire on his desk, wondering if it would attract a paperclip. Mr. Sharma reminded them that the magnetic effect only exists when the switch is closed and current flows through the circuit.
response.summary: Mr. Sharma explains to Rohan and Meera that electric current creates a magnetic field. He clarifies the cause-and-effect relationship and notes that not all metals are magnetic.
